title: Security fixes — the decisions that change what users experience

steps.path: Any chat, when the assistant looks something up online
steps.headline: Should the assistant ask before visiting a website for the first time?
steps.today: The assistant can open any web page to read it without asking, in every permission mode, including Ask first.
steps.problem: A tricked assistant (for example by hidden text on a web page it read) could quietly send your private information out by visiting an address with that information written into it.
steps.proposal: In Ask first mode, the assistant asks the first time it wants to visit each new website, with Allow once and Always allow buttons. Auto-edit and Full Auto behave as today.

options.label: Ask per new site
pros: Closes the quietest way to leak your data, in the mode people pick for safety.
One click per website, and Always allow means you only see it once per site.
cons: Research tasks that visit many sites will ask several times in Ask first mode.

options.label: Ask in every mode
pros: Strongest protection, even in Full Auto.
cons: Full Auto stops being hands-off for any task that uses the web.

options.label: Keep as today
cons: The leak stays open in every mode.

steps.path: Any chat, when the assistant reads a file
steps.headline: Should the assistant ask before reading files outside the project folder?
steps.today: The assistant can read any file on your computer without asking, except a short list of password and key files.
steps.problem: Combined with the web leak above, a tricked assistant could read private documents anywhere on your computer and send them out.
steps.proposal: In Ask first mode, reading a file outside the chat's project folder asks first, with Always allow for that folder. Inside the project nothing changes.

options.label: Ask outside project
pros: Your private files stay private unless you say so.
cons: A chat with no project folder (your home folder) would ask more often.

options.label: Keep as today
cons: Any file not on the short secret list can be read silently.

steps.path: The mode chip under the message box, when switching to Full Auto
steps.headline: Should turning on Full Auto show a short, honest warning the first time?
steps.today: Full Auto runs commands without asking and stops only on a list of obviously dangerous ones, like deleting your home folder.
steps.problem: That list can't catch every harmful command. Users may believe Full Auto is safe because it has safety stops, when the stops are a speed bump, not a guarantee.
steps.proposal: Yes shows a one-time note: 'Full Auto runs commands without asking. It stops on the most dangerous ones, but it can't catch everything. Use it in projects you have backed up.' No keeps today's behaviour.

steps.path: The Always allow choices on a command prompt
steps.headline: Should the one-click Always allow choices be narrower than they are today?
steps.today: Some Always allow choices cover more than their label suggests. Allowing curl also allows uploading files; allowing npm install also allows running a package's own setup scripts.
steps.problem: You might allow something harmless-sounding and unknowingly allow something riskier forever.
steps.proposal: Yes splits these into safer, exact choices (for example 'download with curl' separately from 'send data with curl'). You may see a few more prompts at first. No keeps today's choices.

steps.intro: Using YouCoded from your phone. Only devices on your private Tailscale network can reach it today.

steps.headline: How long must a remote access password be?
steps.today: Any password is accepted, even a very short one. Guessing is now also limited by a lockout we just added.
steps.problem: A short password can still be guessed by someone already on your Tailscale network, and that password controls your whole computer.
steps.proposal: Require a minimum length for new passwords. Existing passwords keep working, with a gentle reminder to change a short one.

options.label: At least 12
pros: Long enough that guessing is hopeless, even with the lockout off.
cons: Slightly more typing the first time you pair a phone.

options.label: At least 8
cons: Relies on the lockout to stop guessing.

options.label: No minimum
cons: A 4-letter password would still be allowed to control the computer.

steps.headline: Should a paired phone stop working after a long time unused?
steps.today: Once a phone is paired, it keeps full control of the computer forever, until you unpair it by hand.
steps.problem: A lost, sold or forgotten phone stays able to control your computer.
steps.proposal: A phone not used for a while is unpaired automatically and has to enter the password again. Phones you use stay paired.

options.label: After 90 days
pros: Phones you use regularly never notice.
cons: A phone you only use on long trips may need the password again.

options.label: After 30 days
cons: More frequent re-pairing for occasional users.

options.label: Never
cons: Forgotten devices stay in control.

steps.path: Pairing the phone to a computer
steps.headline: Should the phone warn when it connects to your computer without encryption?
steps.today: The Android app allows unencrypted connections so it can pair over home Wi-Fi without Tailscale.
steps.problem: On shared Wi-Fi (a café, a dorm), someone nearby could read the pairing password as it travels.
steps.proposal: Choose how strict the phone is about connections that aren't encrypted.

options.label: Warn, then allow
pros: Users on shared Wi-Fi are told to use Tailscale.
cons: One extra notice for people pairing over plain Wi-Fi.

options.label: Tailscale only
cons: Everyone must set up Tailscale before using the phone app.

options.label: Keep as today
cons: Silent risk on shared Wi-Fi.

steps.page: Updates, plugins and the assistant's browser
steps.intro: How new code reaches users' computers, and how the assistant behaves on websites.

steps.path: Theme Builder, Marketplace Publisher, Conversation Search, Page Builder
steps.headline: When should YouCoded's own built-in plugins update on users' computers?
steps.today: Each time the app starts, the built-in plugins update themselves to whatever is newest on GitHub, with no check that it is really yours.
steps.problem: If someone ever got into your GitHub account, every user would get their changes on the next app start, without an app update.
steps.proposal: Choose between fast fixes and a stronger guarantee.

options.label: With app updates
pros: Plugins ride along with the signed, checked app update, so they get the same protection.
Every user on one version has exactly the same plugins.
cons: A plugin fix waits for the next app release.

options.label: Fast, but signed
pros: Only versions you approved and signed are installed.
cons: More work to build, and one more release step for you.

options.label: Keep as today
cons: A GitHub break-in reaches every user without an app update.

steps.path: When the assistant clicks buttons on a website
steps.headline: Should the assistant ask before submitting any form on a website it hasn't used before?
steps.today: The assistant asks before buying, sending, deleting or signing in, but it spots these by English button words like 'Buy' or 'Delete'.
steps.problem: A button labelled 'Continue', or one in another language, can buy or send without the question appearing.
steps.proposal: Yes adds: the first time the assistant submits a form on each website, it asks you, whatever the button says. The word check stays too. No keeps the word check only.

steps.page: Privacy, accounts and the next big step
steps.intro: What users are told, where their reports go, and one larger follow-up project.

steps.headline: Should I draft an accurate rewrite of the privacy policy for your approval?
steps.today: The privacy policy leaves out what the cross-device sync service receives (computer name, project names, a device ID) and the friends 'online' feature, and two sentences in it are inaccurate.
steps.problem: A privacy policy that doesn't match the app is a trust and legal risk, and gets worse as more people use YouCoded.
steps.proposal: Yes: I write a corrected version in plain words and show it to you before anything is published. No: it stays as it is.

steps.path: Settings → Help & feedback → Report a bug
steps.headline: Where should users' bug reports go?
steps.today: A bug report becomes a public GitHub issue. The user sees and can edit it first, and keys are now scrubbed out much more thoroughly.
steps.problem: Reports can still include bits of conversations, file names or project names that the user didn't mean to publish.
steps.proposal: Choose who can read a report.

options.label: Private to you
pros: Nothing a user sends is ever public.
You can still make one public by hand when useful.
cons: Others can't see whether a bug is already reported.
Needs a small server change.

options.label: User chooses
cons: One more choice in the report form; some will pick public without thinking.

options.label: Public, as today
cons: Accidental exposure stays possible.

steps.headline: Should Settings get a 'Sign out of all devices' button?
steps.today: Signing out only signs out the device you are on. The server can now sign an account out everywhere, but there is no button for it.
steps.problem: Someone who thinks their account was used on another device has no way to cut it off.
steps.proposal: Yes adds one button under Account with a confirm step. No leaves it server-only.

steps.headline: Should the Android app's pages move to a safer internal address, even though settings reset once?
steps.today: The Android app loads its screens in a way that lets them read other files inside the app, which is broader than they need.
steps.problem: If someone ever got their own code running in the app's screens, they could read more than they should. No way to do that is known today.
steps.proposal: Yes moves the screens to a locked-down address. Phone users' saved look settings (theme and similar) would need copying across, and I'd attempt that automatically. No leaves it as today.

steps.headline: Should the next project move file previews and Pages to their own walled-off address?
steps.today: We just added a 'only run our own code' lock to the app window, but it has to stay loose on scripts because file previews and Pages share the window's address.
steps.problem: Until they move, the lock can't fully stop outside code if it ever got in.
steps.proposal: Yes makes it the next security project after this release, with its own design review. No leaves the loose lock in place.
